name: Common Atrial Flutter and Macroreentrant and Multifocal Atrial Tachycardias

clinicalPearls: Common (typical) right atrial flutter is a macroreentrant circuit that revolves around the tricuspid valve annulus, passing through the cavotricuspid (sub-Eustachian) isthmus, which is why it is termed cavotricuspid isthmus-dependent flutter and is amenable to interruption at that isthmus (Harrison 22e p.1943).

Counterclockwise rotation of the typical flutter circuit produces the characteristic negative sawtooth flutter waves in the inferior leads II, III, and aVF and positive flutter (P) waves in V1; clockwise (reverse typical) rotation produces the opposite vectors (Harrison 22e p.1943).
The atrial rate in typical flutter is usually 240-300 beats/min but may be slower with atrial disease or antiarrhythmic drugs (Harrison 22e p.1943).
Typical flutter often conducts to the ventricle with 2:1 AV block, yielding a regular tachycardia near 140-150 beats/min, where flutter waves can be obscured within the T wave (Harrison 22e p.1943).
Maneuvers or AV nodal disease/agents that increase AV block raise the conduction ratio and unmask flutter waves, aiding diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1943).
Typical flutter frequently coexists with atrial fibrillation and is associated with atrial scarring from aging or prior cardiac surgery; AF may precede the onset of flutter (Harrison 22e p.1943).

Atrial conduction-slowing antiarrhythmics (flecainide, propafenone, amiodarone) can convert a patient's AF presentation into atrial flutter by promoting reentry while suppressing ectopic triggers (Harrison 22e p.1943).

Atypical (non-cavotricuspid isthmus-dependent) flutters arise in either atrium, are almost universally tied to atrial scar, and are commonly seen after right atriotomy, extensive left atrial ablation for AF, or mitral valve surgery (Harrison 22e p.1943-1944).
Left atrial flutter and perimitral left atrial flutter resemble common flutter clinically but show different P-wave morphologies and can mimic focal atrial tachycardia (Harrison 22e p.1944).

Multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT) is defined by at least three distinct P-wave morphologies with rates typically 100-150 beats/min and is mechanistically attributed to triggered automaticity from multiple atrial foci (Harrison 22e p.1946).
Unlike atrial fibrillation, MAT shows clear isoelectric intervals between P waves and a slower atrial rate, helping distinguish the two (Harrison 22e p.1946).
MAT is characteristically seen in patients with chronic pulmonary disease during acute illness (Harrison 22e p.1946).
harrison.pathophysiology: Macroreentrant atrial tachycardia depends on a large anatomic reentry circuit, frequently involving areas of atrial scar with slow conduction. In common (typical) flutter, the wavefront encircles the tricuspid valve annulus, bounded anteriorly by the annulus and posteriorly by the inferior vena cava and Eustachian ridge, passing through the cavotricuspid isthmus between the IVC and tricuspid annulus. The circuit usually rotates counterclockwise as viewed from the ventricular apex; reversed (clockwise) rotation gives reverse typical flutter. AF and typical flutter are mechanistically interrelated: a line of functional block or coalescence of fibrillatory wavelets around barriers such as the crista terminalis and Eustachian valve may convert AF into organized flutter, and conduction-slowing antiarrhythmics promote this reentry. Atypical flutters are macroreentrant circuits not using the cavotricuspid isthmus, almost always associated with atrial scar. MAT arises from triggered automaticity in multiple atrial foci, producing multiple P-wave morphologies (Harrison 22e p.1943-1946).
additionalDifferentials: Atypical (non-CTI-dependent) atrial flutter vs typical flutter
nonInfectiousMimics: Atrial fibrillation (irregular, no isoelectric baseline between atrial activations) versus MAT (isoelectric intervals present, slower atrial rate)
Focal atrial tachycardia versus left atrial/atypical flutter (distinguished by P-wave morphology and often only by electrophysiology study)
additionalInvestigations: 12-lead ECG to identify sawtooth flutter waves and conduction ratio
Vagal/AV-nodal-blocking maneuvers to unmask flutter waves at higher conduction ratios
Electrophysiology study with electroanatomic mapping to define circuit and confirm mechanism in atypical flutter or to distinguish from focal AT
CHA2DS2-VASc scoring for thromboembolic risk and bleeding-risk assessment
redFlags: Hemodynamic instability with rapid ventricular response (may warrant urgent electrical cardioversion)
Severe symptoms attributable to the arrhythmia
Difficult-to-control ventricular rate, as rate control in flutter is frequently more challenging than in AF
Elevated thromboembolic risk by CHA2DS2-VASc requiring attention before rhythm conversion
harrison.prognosis: Typical flutter is highly treatable, with cavotricuspid isthmus catheter ablation achieving success rates greater than 95% with low complication and recurrence rates; however, up to half of patients undergoing such ablation later develop atrial arrhythmias, most often atrial fibrillation. With antiarrhythmic drug therapy alone, over 70% of patients experience recurrence. MAT prognosis is largely tied to the underlying pulmonary or systemic illness; electrical cardioversion is ineffective for MAT (Harrison 22e p.1944-1946).
pitfalls: In 2:1 conducted flutter, flutter waves hidden in the T wave can be mistaken for another regular narrow-complex tachycardia; failing to use AV-nodal-slowing maneuvers may miss the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1943).
Assuming AF and flutter are independent: antiarrhythmics given for AF (e.g., flecainide, propafenone, amiodarone) may unmask or organize the rhythm into flutter (Harrison 22e p.1943).
Attempting electrical cardioversion for MAT, which is ineffective for this automatic arrhythmia (Harrison 22e p.1946).
Mislabeling atypical/left atrial flutter as focal atrial tachycardia without electrophysiologic confirmation (Harrison 22e p.1944).
Assuming MAT carries the same thromboembolic risk as AF or flutter; in MAT this risk remains unclear and is not considered equivalent (Harrison 22e p.1946).
harrison.severityClassification: No formal severity grading scale; thromboembolic risk in flutter is stratified by the CHA2DS2-VASc score, and hemodynamic stability/symptom severity guides urgency of intervention (Harrison 22e p.1944).
management: Cavotricuspid isthmus catheter ablation as definitive, highly effective therapy for typical flutter
Rate control with beta-blockers or non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers such as diltiazem or verapamil
Restore sinus rhythm by electrical or pharmacological cardioversion, with antiarrhythmic drugs for maintenance where needed
Thromboembolic risk stratification with the CHA2DS2-VASc score and anticoagulation using a direct oral anticoagulant or warfarin
For multifocal atrial tachycardia, treat the underlying pulmonary or metabolic disorder and correct hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia
Surveillance for and management of coexisting atrial fibrillation, which commonly accompanies or follows flutter
Electrophysiology referral with electroanatomic mapping for atypical macroreentrant circuits
